build-17-lazarus.heard: In a village called Bethany, close enough to Jerusalem to walk, there lived two sisters,  Martha and Mary, and their brother Lazarus.  Jesus loved this family. build-11-storm.heard: Evening, on the sea of Galilee. Jesus had been teaching crowds on the shore all day,  story after story, until the light was going and his voice was nearly gone with it. build-110-lords-prayer.heard: One day his followers asked him a simple question, teach us how to pray.  They expected, maybe, a technique, a ritual.  Instead, Jesus gave them a family word. build-111-lilies-and-sparrows.heard: He was talking to people who knew what it was to worry, where the next meal would come  from, whether there would be enough. build-113-where-art-thou.heard: In the beginning there was a garden, and in the garden, peace.  People and God walking together in the cool of the day, with nothing to hide and nothing  to fear. build-114-abraham-sodom.heard: In the heat of the day, three travelers appeared at Abraham's tent.  He did not know at first who they were. Yes.  I will spare it.  He is not wearing God down.  He is discovering how merciful God already is.  How much God would rather spare than destroy.  So Abraham dares one last step. build-115-ram-in-the-thicket.heard: It is one of the hardest stories in the Bible and one of the most misread.  God asks Abraham for the thing he loves most in all the world, his son, and Abraham, trusting  God completely, sets out.  Now watch closely because everything the story means is in how it ends.  Abraham believed, somehow, that God was good, that whatever this was, God could be trusted  with his boy.  So he walked, and he trusted, and he did not let go of that. And as they cloned, the child asked the question that hangs over the whole story.  Behold the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?  My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering.  Father, the boy said, we've got the fire and we've got the wood, but where's the lamb?  And Abraham answered with the line that turns out to be the whole point of the story.  My son, God will provide the lamb himself.  God will provide.  Abraham did not fully understand how.  He only trusted that the God he loved would not, in the end, ask him to lose his son.  And at the very last moment, at the edge of everything, heaven broke open.  Abraham, Abraham.  Here am I.  His name, twice, out of the sky, and the old man answered the way he always had.  Here I am.  Then came the words that ended it.  Lay not thine hand upon the lad, neither do thou anything unto him.  For now I know that thou fierced God.  Don't lay a hand on the boy.  Don't do anything to him at all.  Stop.  God never wanted the child.  He never did.  He stopped Abraham's hand, and right there, caught in a thicket, was a ram.  God's own provision, ready all along.  The boy was safe.  He was always going to be safe.  And the old father gathered his living son into his arms and held him, and wept, and  would not let go.  God had provided.  Abraham, named that place the Lord, will provide, and the name has echoed down every  generation's sense.  In blessing I will bless thee, and in multiplying I will multiply thy seed as the stars of the  heaven, and as the sand which is upon the seashore. It is about a God who provides, who steps in at the last moment with what we could never  provide ourselves.  Centuries later, on another hill nearby, God would provide a lamb again.  This time, his own.  The Lord will provide.  He always has.  God never wanted the child.  He wanted to show he provides.  He stopped the hand and gave the ram, and the boy went home safe.  Where do you most need to trust that the Lord will provide?

build-116-graven-on-his-palms.heard: There is a particular loneliness that comes from feeling forgotten, not hated, just overlooked,  slipped from someone's mind, as if you never really mattered enough to be remembered.  But Zion said, The Lord hath forsaken me, and my Lord hath forgotten me.  That is exactly how God's people felt, and they said it out loud, The Lord has walked  away from me, and my God has forgotten I exist.  And God's answer to that fear is one of the most tender things He ever said.  He points to the strongest, most instinctive love a human being knows.  A mother with her newborn.  Unable to look away.  Unable to forget the child at her breast, even for a moment.  When a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of  her womb.  Yeah, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.  Even if a mother somehow could forget, I never will.  And then he says something almost too intimate to imagine.  He does not just keep you in mind.  He has carved you into his own hands, where he cannot help but see you.  Behold, I have graven thee upon the palms of my hands, thy walls are continually before  me.  Graven engraved, cut in deep, permanent.  Not a note he might lose.  You are written into the very hands of God, and everything about you is always right there  in front of him.  He could not forget you if he tried.  And that changes the person who thought she had been left behind.  The same God she feared had forgotten her was carrying her the whole time.  Her name, her walls, her whole life, held in his hands.  So if you have ever felt like the one who gets forgotten, the one nobody keeps in mind.  Hear this slowly.  You are not out of sight.  You are not out of mind.  You are graven on the hands of God, and he has never once looked away.  God told the ones who felt forgotten that he had carved them into his own hands, always  before his eyes.  You are not overlooked.  Where do you most need to hear that you have not been forgotten?

build-117-hosea-buys-her-back.heard: Love is easy to picture at the beginning.  A man and a woman, hands joined, a covenant freely given, a home with the door open and  the road ahead warm.  That is how God's love for His people began.  But she wondered, not because He stopped being good to her.  He never did, but because her heart drifted.  And Hosea wrote down what she told herself as she went.  I will go after my lovers, that give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, mine  oil and my drink.  I am going after the ones who give me what I want.  She said, my food, my water, my clothes.  She did not think she was walking away from love.  She thought she was walking toward it.  Down the long road toward the cold lights of somewhere else.  Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulterous, according to the love of  the Lord toward the children of Israel, who look to other gods.  And here the story stops being like any other.  God did not tell Hosea to forget her.  Go and love her still.  He said, love her the very way I love a people who leave me.  The whole marriage was a picture of God's own heart, acted out by a man who had to live  it.  By the time he found where she had ended up, she had lost nearly everything.  Brought low, sitting at the edge of a farm marketplace, poor and unseen, a long way  from the home she left.  He could have let her stay lost.  Instead, he came looking.  He walked all that way into a place that was not his own.  Searching the crowd for the one face, he had never stopped loving.  So I bought her to me for fifteen pieces of silver, and for an home of barley, and in half  home of barley.  And when he found her, he did not lecture her.  He paid for her.  Taking pieces of silver and a load of barley, counted out in full, an ordinary price, the  going rate, handed over without a word of argument to buy back her freedom.  He lifted her up off the ground with his own hands, drew his cloak around her shoulders,  and covered her.  No shame thrown at her.  No debt held over her.  Only welcome.  She was his again, not because she earned it, but because he paid.  I will allure her and bring her into the wilderness and speak comfortably unto her.  I will win her back, God says.  I will take her out where it is quiet, away from all the noise, and I will speak to her  tenderly.  Not shouting, not shaming.  Speaking comfortably, the way you talk to someone you are glad to have back.  I will go and return to my first husband, for then was it better with me than now.  I am going back to my first husband, she says, because it was better with me than it is  now.  That is the whole of repentance in one honest sentence, turning around on the road and heading  home.  And I will betrothe unto me forever.  Yeah, I will betrothe unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in loving kindness, and  in mercies.  I will even betrothe unto me in faithfulness, and thou shalt know the Lord.  Betrothed forever.  Not taken back on probation, married again, in righteousness and mercy and faithfulness,  were good.  That is what God says to everyone sure they have wandered too far to be wanted back.  He does not wait at the door with a list of your failures.  He comes looking.  He pays the price himself, and he calls you home.  God dramatized his own love with a marriage.  However far she wandered, he went and bought her back and brought her home.  You are not too far gone to be wanted.  What would it mean to be loved home like that?

build-118-jonah-god-who-relents.heard: God had a hard errand for a man named Jonah. He was to go to Nineveh, a huge, violent,  foreign city, the capital of the empire everyone in Israel was afraid of. And this is how the word came to him.  Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city and cry against it, for their wickedness has come up before me.  Go to that great city and preach against it. God said, because I have seen how bad it has gotten.  Notice what that actually is. It is a warning. God would far rather warn a wicked city than lose it.  But Jonah did not want mercy for people like that. So he ran. He found a ship going the exact opposite way and sailed off,  trying to put an ocean between himself and a god he thought was far too forgiving.  A great storm caught the ship, so fierce the sailors were sure they would all drown.  They cast lots to find out whose fault it was, and the lot fell on Jonah. He knew it already.  And what he told them is the first decent thing he does in the whole book.  Take me up and cast me forth into the sea. So shall the sea be common to you, for I know that for my sake this great tempest is upon you."  Throw me in. He said. The sea will go quiet, because this storm is on me, not on you.  He would rather drown than preach to Nineveh, but he would not let a boat full of strangers go down with him.  So at last they did the only thing left and cast him into the raging sea.  And here is the first surprise of this story. The sea should have been the end of him.  Instead, God sent a great fish, not to punish Jonah, but to catch him and carry him and keep him alive in the deep.  For three days and three nights, in the dark, Jonah finally stopped running. From the belly of the fish he prayed, and his heart,  resentful heart began at last to turn back toward the God who would not let him drown. His prayer ends in four words.  Salvation is of the Lord.  Rescue belongs to God. That is the whole lesson of the fish. And Jonah says it from the one place on Earth where he could not save himself  and had nothing left to bargain with.  Arise, go unto Nineveh, that great city, and preach unto it the preaching that I bid thee.  The fish set him safe on dry land, and God gave him the exact same errand a second time.  No mention of the running, no punishment attached. This time Jonah went. He walked into the great city and cried out his warning.  Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.  Forty more days, and this city is finished. That was the entire sermon. No comfort in it anywhere. No invitation. No offer.  Just to count down. Preached by a man who was hoping it would come true.  And the second surprise is bigger than the first. They listened. From the king on his throne down to the poorest beggar,  the whole city turned. Sackcloth. Fasting. An honest sorrow. Begging God for mercy they knew they did not deserve.  And God, who had been looking for a reason to spare them all along, saw that they turned from their evil, and he relented.  He did not destroy the city. He forgave it. The judgment never fell. And Jonah, watching from a hill outside the walls,  was furious. Listen to why.  I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repentestly of the evil.  I knew it, he says. I knew you were gracious and merciful and slow to anger. I knew you would forgive them.  That is the confession at the bottom of the book. Jonah never ran because he thought God was harsh. He ran because he was afraid God was too good.  And should not I spare Nineveh, that great city wherein are more than 6,000 persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand, and also much cattle?  Should I not spare Nineveh? 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left and the animals too. That is how the book ends.  Not with Jonah answering, but with God still arguing for mercy out loud with his own prophet.  The whole book of Jonah exists to answer one question. Is God eager to destroy or eager to spare? He spared a city of 100,000 strangers the moment they turned.  What would it change to believe God is that quick to forgive?

build-12-bartimaeus.heard: The road out of Jericho on a loud and dusty day. Jericho was the last stop before the climb  up to Jerusalem, and with the Passover feast coming, that road carried half the country.  For a beggar, crowds meant coins. And so a blind man named Bartaiemiyas sat where he  always sat. At the edge of the highway, his ragged cloaks spread across his lap to catch  whatever fell, listening to a thousand feet walk past him. Listening was his whole life.  He knew the road by its sounds. But this day the sound was different. A procession was coming  out of the city, a moving wall of voices, and inside the noise he caught a name. Jesus of  Enazirath was passing by. He had heard the stories everyone had heard. A teacher who opened  deaf ears, who made lepers clean, passing by and never again. A blind man cannot chase  a crowd. All he had was his voice. Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me.  So he used it. He pulled in all the air his body would hold and shout it. Jesus, son of  David, have mercy on me. Catch that title. The crowd called him Jesus of Enazirath, the  man from up north. Son of David was something else entirely. It was the name reserved for  the promised king, the Messiah. Everyone with working eyes saw a traveling teacher. The blind  man was the one who saw who was actually walking past. And the crowd turned on him. Many voices  – Marx says many – told one desperate man to be quiet. Understand why? To them, a beggar  screaming at a famous rabbi was an embarrassment, noise that needed hushing. Respectable people,  telling a man in the dust that his need was bad manners. He shouted louder.  And Jesus stood still. The whole procession stopped around him. Hundreds of feet going quiet  in the dust. Remember where this road was taking him, up to Jerusalem, into the last week of his life.  He was carrying all of that. And one blind beggar's voice, the voice everyone else was trying to shut  off, stopped him in the road. He told them, call him over. Be of good comfort, rise, he callothy.  And listen to the crowd change its tune. The same voices that had been hushing him now crowded in with.  Take heart, get up. He is calling for you. What happened next is one small verse, and it holds the  whole man. He threw off his cloak, jumped up, and came. That cloak was a beggar's entire world. His  coat, his bed at night, the very thing he spread out to catch the coins he lived on.  A blind man who throws his cloak behind him may never find it again. He threw it anyway, coins and  all. He spent everything he owned on the chance that the shout had been heard. So he came, hands out in  front of him, threw a corridor of staring people, and stood breathing hard in front of the man he could  not see. And Jesus asked him one question. What will thou that I should do unto thee?  As if it weren't obvious, a blind man standing in a beggar's tunic. But he asked anyway, because he  wanted the man's own voice, not the crowd's guess about him. Nobody had asked Bartyme as what he wanted  in a very long time. His answer came out in a breath. Rabbi, I want to see. Lord, that I might  receive my sight. Go thy way, thy faith hath made thee whole. And immediately, Mark says, he saw?  The clouds in his eyes cleared like silt settling out of water, and the first thing those new eyes  ever held was daylight on the road ahead. Notice what Jesus told him, your trust did this,  and you are free. Free to go anywhere. And here is the ending Mark wants you to catch.  Free to go anywhere, with brand new eyes and no cloak to go back for. He picked his road,  the one Jesus was walking. He followed him, up the climb toward Jerusalem, staring at everything.  The hills, the faces, his own two hands. The man who had been told to keep quiet  walked in the middle of the procession that had hushed him. The crowd told him to keep quiet,  and he shouted louder. What is the thing you would shout for, if no one could tell you to be quiet?

build-120-job-from-whirlwind.heard: Job was a good man, honest, generous, devoted to God, and for most of his life that goodness  and a happy, prosperous home went together.  And then, in a single devastating stretch, it was all taken, his wealth, his health,  and most unbearable of all, his children.  One of the oldest, hardest questions in the world landed on the best man in it.  Why do good people suffer?  And this is what he said on the day it happened.  Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return to the earth.  The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away.  Blessed be the name of the Lord.  I came into this world with nothing, and I will leave with nothing.  God gave it, and God has taken it, and I will bless him anyway.  He is not calm when he says it.  He has just torn his coat and shaved his head.  He is wrecked and still holding on.  He sat down in the ashes, sick and broken, and he did not pretend to be alright.  He grieved out loud, and scripture never once scolds him for it.  His friends came, and at first they simply sat with him, which was the best thing they  did.  Then they started explaining.  You must have sinned, they said.  This must be your fault.  Their tidy answers only deepen the wound.  But Job would not accept easy lies about God or about himself.  He did something braver than pretending.  He took his anguish straight to God and demanded an answer.  And then, in the middle of it, he said this.  Before I know that my Redeemer liveeth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon  the earth.  I know my Redeemer is alive.  He says, and one day he will stand right here on this earth.  That is a man in the ashes with nothing left, saying it out loud.  He does not understand a thing that is happening to him, and he still knows who is coming.  And God answered, though not in the way anyone expected, out of a great whirlwind,  the maker of everything finally spoke.  Where was thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?  Declare if thou hast understanding.  Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?  It sounds like a rebuke, and it is not.  God is doing something gentler than that.  He is taking a man who has shrunk down to the size of his own pain and slowly widening  the room.  When the Morning Stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy, the Morning  Stars sang together and all the sons of God shouted for joy.  That is God describing the day the world was made, and it is not a lecture about power.  It is a memory, and it is full of gladness.  Can't thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades or loose the bands of Orion?  Can you tie up the Pleiades?  God asks or unfastenerions built.  On and on it goes the sea, the snow, the wild donkey, the horse, the hawk.  After after chapter of a world far bigger and stranger and kinder than the tidy little  courtroom jobs friends had built.  Behold, I am vile.  What shall I answer thee?  I will lay mine hand upon my mouth.  Once have I spoken, but I will not answer yet twice, but I will proceed no further.  I have nothing to say, job answers.  I am putting my hand over my mouth.  I have said my peace, and I will not say it again.  Not beaten, quieted.  God never explained why.  Instead he showed job the sea and the stars, and the wild goodness of a world job could never  have made or held.  And somehow it was enough.  I have heard of thee by the hearing of the year, but now mine I see thee.  I had only ever heard about you, Job says.  Now I have seen you with my own eyes.  That is the ending.  Not because he got his answer, but because he got God himself.  The suffering was never fully explained, not to Job and not to us.  But Job was no longer alone in it.  The God he thought had abandoned him had come near, and that nearness was the answer his  grief actually needed.  Job's comfort was never a reason for his pain.  It was a person who showed up in it.  If you are in the ashes right now, the promise is not a tidy explanation.  It is that God draws near to the broken.  Where do you most need him to show up?

build-121-salt-and-light.heard: Jesus sat on a green hillside above the sea of Galilee, an ordinary crowd gathered on  the grass around him, fishermen, mothers, farmers, children, and to these plain, unremarkable  people he said something astonishing about who they were.  He began with salt.  Yea the salt of the earth, but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it  be salted?  It is then sporth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of  men.  In that world salt was precious.  It kept food from spoiling, and it made plain things taste good.  That he told them, is what you are.  You keep the world from going bad, and you bring out the good in it.  You matter that much.  But salt has one job, and if it goes flat and loses its flavour it is no use to anyone.  It just gets swept out and walked over.  He was not threatening them.  He was telling them not to waste what they were.  Stay salty.  Stay yourselves.  Yea the light of the world.  A city that is set on and hill cannot be hit.  When he pointed them to light, a town built up on a hilltop, its lamps lit at dusk, can  be seen for miles.  There is no hiding it.  That, he said, is you.  Not something the world should have to squint to find, but a light set up where everyone can  see.  Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick, and it give  it light unto all that are in the house.  Nobody lights a lamp and then hides it under a basket.  That would be pointless, smothering the very thing they lit it for.  You set it up high on a stand, so its light reaches into every corner and everyone in  the house can see.  Your goodness was never meant to be hidden away.  It was meant to give light to the people around you.  Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works and glorify your father  which is in heaven.  So let it shine, he said.  Live openly good, kind, honest, generous, right out where people can see it.  But notice the reason, not so they will admire you, so that when they see the good you do,  their eyes will lift past you to God, and they will love him for it.  Your light is not about you at all.  It points home to your father.  That is the whole charge, and it is a gentle one.  You do not have to become something you are not.  You already are salt.  You already are light.  Just don't lose your savor, and don't hide your lamp.  Go out, stay bright, and be exactly what the world needs.  You are the salt of the earth.  You are the light of the world.  Not someday, if you are good enough, right now, as you are.  Where could your light give someone else a little more of God today?

build-122-mote-and-beam.heard: Of all the things Jesus taught on that hillside, one of them cuts straight to how we treat each other, and it starts with a warning we would rather skip.  Judge not that ye be not judged.  For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged.  We are experts at spotting the small faults in someone else, a tiny speck, a moat in our brother's eye, and we cannot wait to point it out.  But Jesus drew a picture so absurd it makes you laugh, a man fussing over a speck of sawdust in someone else's eye, while an entire wooden beam is sticking straight out of his own.  He cannot even see straight. The beam is in the way of everything he does, and yet he is completely sure that he is the one who ought to be fixing other people.  And then, if we are honest, the moment finally comes when we catch sight of the beam, not hiss, ours, the one we had been carrying the whole time.  Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye, and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the moat out of thy brother's eye.  Notice he does not say ignore your brother's speck. He says deal with your own beam first, and then you will actually be able to help him gently, instead of just condemning him.  The goal was never to stop caring about each other. It was to come to each other humble instead of superior, as one flawed person helping another, not a judge passing a sentence.  The measure you use is the measure you will get back. So Jesus offers a better one, mercy, deal honestly with yourself, and you will be amazed how much patience you suddenly have for everyone else.  Jesus was not telling us to stop seeing clearly. He was telling us where to start with the beam in our own eye. Deal with that, and our eyes for other people fill with mercy instead of judgment.  Who's speck have you been watching while a beam waited in your own eye?

build-123-golden-rule.heard: Of everything Jesus taught on that hillside, He gave the whole law of how to treat each other in a single sentence.  One so simple a child can live it, and so deep it holds up everything else.  Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that man should do to you, d even so to them, for this is the law and the prophets.  Every one of us already knows how we long to be treated, to be seen when we are tired, to be fed when we are hungry, to be forgiven when we have failed.  That longing is not selfish, it is the measuring line.  So Jesus turns it outward.  The bread you wish someone would hand you when you are empty, handed to the next person you find standing at your door with nothing.  The cool drink you would want on a long, dusty road. Be the one who holds it out to the stranger before he even thinks to ask.  And the mercy you would ache for if it were your own mistake laid bare. Give that first, and give it fully to the person who wronged you.  When someone stumbles on the road ahead of you, do not step around him. Lift him the way you would want to be lifted if it were your own knees in the dust.  Give, and it shall be given unto you. Good measure, press down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom.  That is the quiet secret of it. A life poured out in kindness does not run dry.  It comes back around, table to table, neighbor to neighbor, until a whole village is carrying one another.  The golden rule is not a weight Jesus laid on us.  It is the shortest way to everything the law was ever trying to teach.  Treat others the way you long to be treated, and you will have kept nearly all of it at once.  Jesus folded the whole law into one line. You can start living today. Before you decide how to treat someone, picture how you would want to be treated in their place.  Then simply do that. Who is the one person? This week, you could treat the way you have always wished someone would treat you.  Someone would treat you.

build-124-love-your-enemies.heard: On a green hillside above the Sea of Galilee, Jesus sat down to teach, and a whole countryside  climbed up to listen.  He was walking through the old sayings one at a time.  You have heard it said, and then he came to the hardest one of all.  What to do with an enemy.  Everyone on that hillside knew the old arithmetic.  Love the people who love you.  Keep your guard up against the ones who don't.  It felt fair.  It felt safe.  And then Jesus said this.  But I say unto you, love your enemies.  Bless them that curse you.  Do good to them that hate you.  And pray for them which despitefully use you and persecute you.  Not tolerate them.  Not stay out of their way.  Bless.  Do good.  Pray.  Every one of those is something you go and do.  Amstrate at the person who has earned none of it.  Picture a farmer whose neighbor has wronged him.  The fence knocked down.  The insult at the well.  Years of cold looks across one stone wall.  He has every right to answer coldness with coldness.  That is the old arithmetic and nobody would blame him for it.  Instead, when his neighbor's wall gives way in the reins, he walks over quietly and  starts lifting stones.  And at night, when the work is done and no one is watching, he does the thing Jesus  asked that no one ever sees.  By the light of his lamp, he prays for the man across the wall, not about him.  For him, by name.  Why would Jesus ask for something this unreasonable?  He was not pretending enemies don't hurt.  He gave his reason on the same hillside and the reason changes everything.  That he may be the children of your father which is in heaven.  For he mocketh his son to rise on the evil and on the good and sendeth rain on the Justin  on the unjust.  Look at the sky.  He was saying.  Your father's son came up this morning over every field in the valley, the kind man's and  the cruel man's alike.  His rain waters both.  Loving an enemy is not unnatural.  In this family, it is the resemblance.  Anyone can love the people who love them back.  Jesus pointed out that even the tax collectors manage that much.  The love that marks you as your father's child is the love that is not owed.  And sometimes, slowly, it wins what coldness never could.  The wall between two houses becomes the place where they meet.  Jesus never said your enemy deserves it.  He said this is how the family likeness shows.  Who was the hardest person in your life to bless?  What might change if, tonight, you prayed for them by name?

build-125-i-never-knew-you.heard: Jesus warned that saying the right words is not the same as knowing Him.  The door is not opened by a name we repeat.  Not everyone that seth unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven,  but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven.  He described a day when many will point to what they did, prophecies, miracles, works done in his name.  Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name?  And in thy name have cast out devils.  And in thy name done many wonderful works.  And then the honest part, knowing Him matters more than sounding like we do.  And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you, depart from me, ye that work iniquity.  This is not a threat to scare you.  It is an invitation to be known, to walk with Him, not just speak His name.  He wants to know you, not just be named by you.  Come close and let Him know you.

build-126-by-their-fruits.heard: Jesus taught how to tell what is true. Look at what grows from it.  Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are  ravening wolves. A tree shows what it is by what it bears. You don't guess at a tree  by its bark. You shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns,  or figs of thistles. Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit, but a corrupt  tree bringeth forth evil fruit. The good and the rotten cannot switch places. What is inside  comes out in the open. Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down and cast  into the fire. Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them. What grows from a life with  him is good fruit. Love, kindness, truth. Abide in him and let it show.

build-127-the-strait-gate.heard: Jesus stood before the crowd and described two roads, two ways that every person gets to choose.  One road looks easy. The gate is wide, the path is broad, and a lot of people walk that way.  The other road looks harder. The gate is narrow, the path is tight, and far fewer find it.  Enter ye in at the straight gate, for wide is the gate, and broad is the way that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in their at.  Because straight is the gate, and narrow is the way which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.  He wasn't describing geography. He was describing a decision.  A narrow gate that leads to life, found by the few who choose it.  There are two gates in one choice. He said the narrow way is worth finding. Step through.

build-128-famine-of-hearing.heard: The prophet Amos carried a warning from the Lord, not about food, but about something  people would miss even more.  A day would come when God's voice would seem far away, not because he stopped speaking,  but because people stopped being able to hear.  Behold, the days come, set the Lord God that I will send a famine in the land, not  a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord.  And they shall wander from sea to sea, and from the North even to the East, they shall  run to and fro to seek the word of the Lord, and shall not find it.  The deepest hunger isn't in the stomach.  It's the ache of a soul that can't find a word from God.  The cure was never far.  It was to listen while his voice could still be heard.  When his word is near, don't let it pass.  Listen now, the famine is the silence we choose.

build-129-nazareth-only-a-few.heard: Jesus went back to Nazareth, the town that watched him grow up. He taught in the synagogue.  But the people who'd known him as a boy couldn't believe. They took offense at him, and their unbelief became a wall.  He could do only a few mighty works there, not because his power ran out, but because they wouldn't receive it.  And he could there do no mighty work, save that he laid his hands upon a few sick folk, and healed them.  And he marveled because of their unbelief.  He still healed the few who came. Even amazement at their doubt didn't stop his mercy.  Faith opens the door, where people believed, even a little, he worked.  He healed the few who reached out. The door is the same today, believe, and let him work.

build-13-roof.heard: Capernaum, on the north shore of the sea of Galilee. Jesus was home, and the word got  out. By the time four men came up the street carrying their friend on a sleeping mat, one  at each corner, the house he was teaching in had already swallowed half the town. The  man on the mat was paralyzed. He could not walk to Jesus. So the people who loved him  decided he would get there anyway. But the doorway was a wall of backs. People packed the  room, packed the doorway, spilled into the street. No one was giving up a spot, not even for a man  on a mat. For friends stood their breathing hard, holding their friend, staring at an impossible  crowd, and then one of them looked up, at the roof. Here is something worth knowing. Houses  there had flat roofs of packed clay over reeds and beams, with a stairway up the outside wall.  You could dig through one with your hands in a few minutes, and patch it in a day,  which is exactly what they did. For men on a stranger's roof, tearing through the clay,  coughing in the dust, grinning at each other like men doing something magnificent and slightly insane.  Below them, in the middle of the sermon, the ceiling cracked open. Daylight poured into the  dark room through falling dust and straw. And down through that column of light, swaying on four  ropes, lowered with enormous care, came a man on a mat, landing right at the feet of Jesus.  Now listen to what the story says next, because it is easy to miss. When Jesus saw their faith,  theirs, the friends, the four sweat-streaked faces ringing the hole in the roof, the man on the mat  hadn't said a word, his friends' faith counted for him. He was carried there, and heaven honored the  carrying. And Jesus looked at the man lying in the dusty light, a man braced for words about his  legs, and the first thing he said was not about his legs at all. Son, thy sins be forgiven thee.  The first word was son, not a diagnosis, not a lecture about his legs. Son, and then forgiveness.  In that world, everyone assumed a body like his was the proof of some hidden guilt. He had  carried the shame along with the paralysis his whole life. Jesus went to the deepest wound first.  His legs had not moved yet, and it was already the miracle. But in the corner sat the scribes,  the religious experts, and nothing about this made them glad. They didn't say a word out loud.  They reasoned it in their hearts, this is blasphemy. No one can forgive sins, but God alone. And on  the logic, they were exactly right. That was the point they refused to see. Why does this man  thus speak blasphemies? Who can forgive sins but God only? And then came the strangest moment in that  room, stranger than the ceiling. Jesus knew what they were thinking. They had said nothing,  and he answered them anyway. Whether is it easier to say to the sick of the palsy,  thy sins be forgiven thee, or to say, arise, and take up thy bed, and walk?  He was asking them, which is easier to say. Anyone can announce that sins are forgiven.  No one can check. But tell a paralyzed man to stand, and everyone in the room finds out in a  second what your words are worth. So, he said, so that you will know the forgiveness was real.  Watch this. He turned back to the man on the mat.  I say unto thee, arise, and take up thy bed, and go thy way into thine house.  And immediately he did. He stood, on legs trembling like a newborn colts, while the crowd pulled back  and the dust floated in the light. Then he bent down, rolled up his mat, and tucked it under his arm.  The bed that had carried him, he carried home. He walked out the door in front of everyone,  through the same crowd that had no room for him an hour before. They made room now.  Mark says they were all amazed, and gave the glory to God, and said to each other,  we have never seen anything like this. And up on the roofline, for filthy, grinning friends pounded  each other's shoulders, and laughed toward heaven. We never saw it on this fashion.  For people tore a roof open because their friend could not get there alone. His faith didn't carry  him that day. There's did, and heaven counted it. So here is the question this story leaves behind.  Where do you find yourself in that room? On the mat, or holding a rope?

build-130-what-manner-of-spirit.heard: As Jesus traveled toward Jerusalem, a Samaritan village refused to welcome him.  The disciples James and John were hot with anger.  They asked if they should call down fire from heaven to burn the place.  They wanted judgment.  Jesus turned and rebuked them, not the village, but his own disciples' hearts.  He know not what manner of spirit ye are of.  For the Son of Man is not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them.  He didn't come to burn.  He came to rescue.  The fire in the disciples' hearts was the wrong kind.  Anger that wants to destroy isn't from him.  The Spirit he brings saves.  He came to save, not to burn.  Let his spirit, the saving one, shape yours.

build-131-scribe-near-the-kingdom.heard: A teacher of the law came to Jesus with a real question, not a trap, which commandment  matters most of all.  Jesus answered without hesitation, love God with everything you are, and love your  neighbor as yourself.  Everything else hangs on those too.  The scribe agreed and added something honest to love God and neighbor is worth more than  any burn offering.  Jesus looked at him and saw a man thinking clearly with an open heart.  Thou art not far from the kingdom of God.  Not far.  The man was close, a step from the door, and no one dared question Jesus after that.  You may be closer than you think.  Love God, love your neighbor, and step through the door.

build-132-forbid-him-not.heard: John came to Jesus with a complaint.  They'd seen someone driving out demons using Jesus' name,  and the man wasn't one of their group, so they told him to stop.  John thought he was protecting the cause.  The man wasn't with them, so he shouldn't be using the name.  Jesus corrected the instinct.  Don't stop him.  Anyone doing good in my name isn't against you.  Forbid him not, for there is no man which shall do a miracle in my name  that can lightly speak evil of me.  For he that is not against us is on our part.  Whoever gives a cup of water in his name won't lose his reward.  The work isn't about belonging to a team, it's about him.  John learned a lesson that day.  The kingdom is bigger than the inner circle.  Don't draw the circle too small.  Whoever works in his name is on your side.

build-133-many-mansions.heard: Jesus was preparing His disciples for a hard goodbye. His words could have brought fear.  Instead, they brought comfort. Don't let your heart be troubled. He said, Trust God, trust me.  He described a home they couldn't see yet, a place he was going to make ready for them, room for each one.  Let not your heart be troubled. You believe in God. Believe also in me.  In my father's house are many mansions. If it were not so, I would have told you.  I go to prepare a place for you.  And then the promise that undoes every fear. I'm coming back. I'll bring you to myself,  so you're where I am.  Not a vague hope. A prepared place. A return. A reunion.  He's preparing a place. And he's coming back for you. Don't let your heart be troubled.

build-134-other-sheep-i-have.heard: Jesus used to picture His listeners knew well a shepherd and his sheep.  He was the good shepherd and they were his flock.  But He said the flock was bigger than the people standing there.  There were other sheep, not of that pen, that He would also bring.  They would hear His voice and the result would be one flock, one shepherd.  And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold, them also I must bring,  and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd.  Not divided by nation or wall, one voice, one care, one shepherd over all who listen.  Whoever hears Him belongs, wherever they are from.  His voice reaches further than you think.  Hear Him, and you're in the fold.

build-135-rainbow-covenant.heard: The rain had stopped. For the better part of a year, one family and a great wooden boat  full of animals had ridden out the end of the world they knew. Then one morning the  arc set still on a mountainside, and the Earth lay quiet and washed and knew.  Noah and his family stepped out onto wet grass under an open sky. There were eight  of them, and everything they had ever known was gone. The whole human story was  starting over, and the very first thing God said to them was not a warning.  Be fruitful and multiply and replenish the Earth.  Philip back up, go live. Eight people standing in the wreckage of a drowned  world, and God's opening word to them is a blessing and a future. But one heavy  question still hung over at all. Could anyone trust the sky again? Here is the  first thing Noah built in the new world. Not a house, not a fence. He gathered stones  and built an altar, and he gave thanks. And God answered that small smoking altar  with a promise about the whole future. While the earth remaineth seed time and  harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease.  Planting time and gathering time, winter and summer, morning and night. The world would  keep its rhythm for as long as it stands. But God was not finished, because he knew  something about these eight people. He knew what rain now meant to them. Think about  the first time clouds rolled in after the flood. For Noah's family, a dark sky was no  longer just weather. It was the memory of everything they had lost. And God did not  scold them for being afraid. He moved to meet the fear.  And I, behold, I establish my covenant with you, and with your seed after you.  A covenant is the Bible's most serious word for a promise, one that binds the person who  makes it. And notice who is doing the binding here. Noah is not asked to promise anything,  sign anything, or earn anything. God binds himself one way for free to Noah, to his children,  and to every living creature that walked off that boat.  And I will establish my covenant with you. Neither shall all flesh be cut off any more by the waters  of a flood. Neither shall there any more be a flood to destroy the earth.  Never again. That is the whole promise, with no conditions attached, and no expiration date.  And then God does something wonderfully tender. He gives the promise a sign you can see with your eyes.  I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.  The word there is simply bow, and it is the same word the Bible uses for a battle bow,  a weapon of war. God hangs a bow in the clouds, unstrung, aimed away from the earth. It is the  picture of a warrior hanging up his weapon on the wall. The storm between heaven and earth is over.  And the bow shall be in the cloud, and I will look upon it, that I may remember the everlasting  covenant between God and every living creature of all flesh that is upon the earth.  Did you catch who the sign is for? God set the reminder where he would see it. The rainbow is the  string God tied around his own finger. Before it ever comforts you, it is his own promise,  kept deliberately in his own sight. And the promise held. Rain has come and gone for thousands of years  since that mountainside. And when the shower passes, the same sign still climbs the sky.  Children point at it. Nobody runs from it. That is what it feels like to live inside a promise  God is keeping. This is the God the whole story has been about. A God who knows exactly what frightens  his people and answers fear with beauty instead of blame. A God who binds himself with promises  and then keeps them. He has not changed. After the flood, God made a one-way promise  and hung the reminder where he himself would see it. The next rainbow you see is God remembering.  What might change for you if you believed he keeps his promises?

build-136-healed-in-two-touches.heard: Friends brought a blind man to Jesus and Beth Ceta and begged him just to touch him.  Jesus took the man by the hand and walked him outside the village.  He spit on the man's eyes and laid his hands on him, then asked if he could see anything yet.  The man looked up and said the strangest thing.  He could see, but only half way.  People looked like trees walking around.  So Jesus put his hands on the man's eyes a second time and told him to look up again.  And this time he saw everything clearly, every face, every leaf.  The second touch finished what the first had started.  Neither go into the town nor tell it to any in the town.  Maybe your faith came in stages too.  He is patient enough to touch you twice.

build-137-one-as-we-are-one.heard: The night before he died, Jesus stopped to pray, and in that prayer, He prayed for someone  you might not expect, for everyone who would ever believe.  That includes you.  Neither pray I for these alone, but for them also which shall believe on me through their  word, that they all may be one, as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they  also may be one in us.  Listen to how he asks.  He prays that his followers will be one, the same way he and his father are one.  If that oneness meant one single being, this prayer would be asking millions of believers  to melt into one person.  It doesn't ask that.  It asks for perfect unity between distinct persons.  And the glory which thou gavest me I have given them, that they may be one, even as we  are one, I in them, and thou in me, that they may be made perfect in one.  The Father and the Son are perfectly one, one in purpose, one in love, one in glory,  two persons, one heart, and Jesus prayed that you would be brought into that same oneness.  The night before he died, he prayed for you, that you would be one with them, as they  are one with each other.

build-137-stephen-sees-him-standing.heard: The council was furious. They dragged Stephen out and hurled stones.  But Stephen was looking somewhere else entirely.  Full of the Holy Ghost, he gazed up into heaven and saw the glory of God.  Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing on the right hand of God.  Not sitting, standing, as if ready to receive the one they were killing.  The vision held him steady while the stones fell. He saw his Savior standing for him.  He stands for you too. Whatever falls on you today, you are not alone.

build-138-his-offspring.heard: Paul stood in the middle of Athens, surrounded by statues to every God they could think of,  and one altar that simply said to the unknown God.  He told them they were already closer than they knew.  The God they had left unnamed made the whole world, and He is not far from any of us.  In him, Paul said, we live and move and have our being.  He even quoted their own poets.  We are His children.  For in him we live and move and have our being, as certain also of your own poets have said,  for we are also His offspring.  God overlooked the times of ignorance before, Paul said, but now He commands all men everywhere  to repent.  The unknown God was never unknown to him.  He had been near the whole time. build-139-lamp-on-a-stand.heard: Jesus was teaching a crowd on a mountainside.  He told them who they were before he told them what to do.  Ye are the light of the world. build-14-ten-lepers.heard: On the way to Jerusalem, Jesus walked the borderland between Samaria and Galilee, the  scene between two peoples who despised each other. Keep that seam in mind. build-140-road-runs-both-ways.heard: Jesus told a story about a father and two sons.  The younger one wanted a share of the inheritance now, and he got it.  And he said, a certain man had two sons. build-141-bread-of-life.heard: A crowd had followed Jesus after he fed thousands with a few loaves.  They wanted more bread. He gave them something deeper.  I am the bread of life. build-142-light-of-the-world.heard: Jesus stood among the temple courts and spoke into the noise of the crowd.  I am the light of the world, He that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life." build-143-i-am-the-door.heard: Jesus used a picture the crowd knew well, a sheep fold with one opening, and a shepherd who guards it.  Verily, verily, I say unto you, I am the door of the sheep. build-144-resurrection-and-the-life.heard: Lazarus had been in the tomb for days. His sister Martha came to Jesus, heavy with grief, but still full of faith. build-145-way-truth-life.heard: In the upper room, the night before the cross, Jesus told his disciples he was going to prepare a place for them. build-147-joseph-forgives.heard: Years before, Joseph's own brothers had sold him into slavery out of jealousy.  Now he was second only to Pharaoh in all Egypt.  When the brothers came begging for food in the famine, they didn't recognize the brother they betrayed.  Then he sent every Egyptian out of the room and told them.  I am Joseph your brother, whom he sold into Egypt.  I'm Joseph, your brother, the one you sold. He didn't soften it, and he didn't skip it.  He said the worst thing they ever did straight to their faces, and then he kept talking.  Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me hither, for God did send me before you to preserve life.  Don't tear yourselves up over it, he said. Don't be angry at yourselves that you sold me here.  God sent me ahead of you to keep people alive.  He gave them the one thing they could not give themselves, permission to stop hating themselves.  Much later, when their father died and the brothers feared revenge, Joseph spoke the line that closes the wound.  But as for you, he thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.  You meant it for evil, he told them. I'm not going to call it anything else.  But God meant it for good, and look what came of it, a whole lot of people are still alive.  He didn't pretend it hadn't hurt. build-15-centurion.heard: This is Capiarnaeum, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus often stayed and  taught.  It was also filled with Roman soldiers, the army that had conquered these people and  now ruled them by force.  So the Jews here had every reason to hate Rome.  Hold on to that, because the man this story is about where is a Roman uniform.  In one of those Roman houses, a young servant was dying.  His body had gone stiff and useless, and he was in terrible pain.  A servant in those days was treated as property.  If he died, most masters would simply replace him.  But this master could not bring himself to walk away.  The master was a centurion, a Roman officer in command of a hundred soldiers.  A powerful man into the Jews, the enemy.  Yet he left his house and went straight to Jesus, a Jewish teacher, to beg for help, not  for himself, not even for his own son, for a servant.  He came humbly, head bowed, and told Jesus the plain truth.  His servant was at home, unable to move in agony.  Did Jesus help him?  Jesus did not hesitate for a moment.  He answered that he would go to the house himself.  I will come and heal him.  Stop and see what that means.  Jesus was willing to walk into the home of a Roman, the enemy, for the sake of one dying  servant nobody else valued.  That is who Jesus is.  But the officer stopped him.  Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof, but speak the word only, and  my servant shall be healed.  Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, he said.  Only say the word, and my servant will be healed.  He was not just being polite.  He truly believed Jesus did not need to be there at all.  He believed that Jesus' word, by itself, was enough.  And he explained why, in the only language a soldier knows.  For I am a man under authority, having soldiers under me, and I say to this man, go, and he  goeth, and to another come, and he comeeth, and to my servant do this.  And he doeth it.  I am a man under authority, he said.  I tell one soldier, go, and he goes.  I tell another, come, and he comes.  I tell my servant to do a thing, and it is done.  He never has to go himself.  His word alone carries his power across the whole camp.  He was certain Jesus' word worked the same way, that it could reach across the town and  heal on its own.  And this amazed Jesus.  The gospels almost never say that anyone surprised him, yet the faith of this Roman outsider  stopped him.  He turned to the crowd, and said,  Veraecly I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.  In plain words, no one among his own people, the ones who should have known God best, had  ever trusted him the way this outsider, just had.  Then Jesus opened heaven wider than anyone listening expected.  And I say unto you, that many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down  with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.  He meant that people from every nation on earth would be welcomed to God's table.  What brings you in is not where you were born, or which group you belong to.  It is whether you trust Him.  When Jesus turned back to the soldier and gave him the one thing He had asked for, a  single word.  Go thy way, and as thou hast believed, so be it done unto thee.  Go home.  It has already happened, just as you trusted it would.  No touch, no visit, only His word sent across the town.  And in that very hour, far away in the Roman house, the young servant drew a deep, clean  breath.  The color flowed back into his face, his body loosened, and he sat up completely well.  No one was in the room with him.  He was made whole by nothing but the word of a man he had never even met.  When the officer reached home, his servant rose to meet him at the door, alive and well.  This hardened soldier, who commanded a hundred men, came apart.  He had trusted Jesus' word, and the word had been enough.  This Roman soldier trusted Jesus before he saw any proof at all.  Is there something in your life you would place in Jesus' hands like that?  Stay honest word.

build-152-revealeth-his-secret.heard: The man God chose to speak through was not a king or a priest.  He was a herdsman out with his flock on the hills, a plain working man.  God has always loved to call ordinary people to carry extraordinary words.  And one day the word of the Lord came to him, not his own idea, not a clever guess about  what was coming, but a message given to him from God, as real and clear as a voice carried  on the wind.  Here is something studying about the way God works.  Before he acts, he tells someone.  He does not move against his people in the dark, with no warning.  He opens his plans to a servant he can trust to pass them on.  Surely the Lord God will do nothing, but he revioleth his secret unto his servants the prophets.  Think about what that means.  The God who holds everything together chooses to let people in on what he is about to do.  He trusts his real plan to a prophet, the way a father warns his household before the storm arrives.  So the prophet does not keep it to himself.  He goes down to where the people are, to the gate and the market, and he says out loud the  very thing God told him, whether the crowd wants to hear it or not.  And this is a mercy, not a threat.  A people who are warned can still turn.  They can get ready, mend what is broken, and come home in time.  No one who listened was ever caught by surprise.  The lion hath roared, who will not fear?  The Lord God has spoken, who can but prophesy?  When God has truly spoken, the prophet cannot stay silent.  Any more than you could ignore a lion roaring close beside you.  The message is not his to soften or hold back.  He simply has to say it.  And that is the quiet comfort in this verse.  God still does not leave his people guessing.  He still opens his plans to living prophets, so that anyone willing to listen can hear where  he is going before he gets there.  So the only question is a gentle one.  Are you listening for it?  God does nothing without first telling his servants the prophets.  He warns before he acts, because he wants his people ready, not surprised.  He still speaks this way.  Are you listening?

build-153-restitution.heard: After a lame man was healed at the temple gate, a crowd came running, amazed.  And Peter, a fisherman-turned-preacher, stood up among them to explain what they had really  just seen.  Silver and gold have I none.  But such as I have give I thee, in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk.  I have no money, Peter told him.  But what I do have, I give you.  And in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, he told a man who had never walked to stand  up.  He had nothing in his pockets, and he gave away the only thing he had that was worth anything.  His message was not complicated.  Turn back to God, he said, Change your direction, let your wrongs be wiped away, and something  good will follow.  That someday far off, but seasons of relief, sent from God himself.  Picture that word, refreshing, like cool rain on cracked ground, like a deep breath after  a long, hard road.  That is what God longs to pour out on people who simply turn back toward him.  Repent you therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out when the times  of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord.  But Peter pointed to something even larger than one person's fresh start.  He spoke of a day when everything that has gone wrong with the world would finally be  set right, a healing not only of people, but of all things.  Until that day, he said, Heaven itself is keeping the promise safe.  The way you hold back the best gift for exactly the right moment.  It is coming, but at the appointed time, and not a moment before.  And this was not some new idea Peter dreamed up.  Every true prophet, all the way back to the beginning, had promised the very same thing,  a great restoring, a putting right of everything spoken of since the world began.  Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God has  spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.  Restitution means giving back what was lost, restoring what was broken to the way it was  always meant to be, not patched up, not almost, made whole, made new, every part of it.  So this verse is a promise you can lean your full weight on.  The world is not just sliding into ruin.  It is heading toward a restoration God has planned from the very start.  So the only question is a hopeful one.  Will you turn and be part of the refreshing when it comes?  The world is not ending in ruin.  It is heading toward a restoration of all things, promised by every prophet since the  beginning.  Turn back to God and be refreshed.  Will you be ready for the restoring?

build-154-everlasting-gospel.heard: 4 long stretches of history, whole peoples lived without it. The good news about God,  misplaced, buried, or never yet heard. Men reached for heaven in the dark and could not  quite find the way. And then, in a vision, John of Patmos saw heaven open and something  calm, not an army, not a storm, but an angel sent on an errand of mercy, carrying a message  meant for the whole earth. The angel flew across the height of heaven for all to see,  holding out an open book, the good news about God, ready to be given back to a world that  had lost hold of it.  And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach  unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and town, and people.  Notice the word, everlasting. This good news was never really invented or improved by anyone.  It is older than the nations, the same true message from the beginning, carried down from  heaven and offered fresh again. And notice who it is for, not one favored people, not  one language or land, but every nation, every family, every town. No one is too far away,  too foreign, or too late to be handed this. The angel's call is simple and clean. Honor  God, give him the glory and worship the one who made it all, the heavens, the earth, the sea,  and every spring of water. Turn your face back toward your maker.  Saying with a loud voice, fear God, and give glory to him, for the hour of his judgment is come,  worship him that made heaven and earth, and the sea, and the fountains of waters.  It is a call to come home to the God of creation, the same God who set the stars in place and filled  the seas. Not a distant idea, but the maker of the very ground under your feet, quietly asking for  your heart. So here is the quiet wonder of this verse. The good news was never abandoned for good.  Heaven sent it out again on purpose for everyone, which means it was sent for you, too. So the only  question is a gentle one. Will you receive it? The gospel was never lost for good. Heaven sent an angel  to carry it back to every nation, kindred and tongue, everlasting and meant for you. Will you receive it?

build-155-falling-away.heard: The young believers in Thessalonica were rattled.  Rumors were flying that the great day of the Lord had already come, and they were frightened  and confused.  So Paul sat down to write them a steadying letter.  His first word to them was calm.  Do not let yourselves be shaken or alarmed.  He said, By every excited rumor and second hand report, or stampede it into fear by things  you cannot even trace to their source.  He wanted them anchored, not tossed around by the loudest voice in the room.  Feelings in hearsay are not the same as truth, and a frightened crowd is rarely a wise one.  That ye be not soon shaken in mind, or be troubled, neither by spirit, nor by word, nor  by letter as from us, as that the day of Christ is at hand.  Then Paul told them plainly what to watch for.  That day, he said, would not arrive until something else happened first, and it was sobering.  Before the end, there would come a falling away.  Adrifting from the truth, a dimming of the light that had been lit, many hearts over time,  turning away from what the apostles had actually given them, until much of it was lost from  view.  But here is the part that turns dread into hope.  Paul is telling them ahead of time.  A falling away would not mean God had failed, or his plan had broken.  It would mean the very thing he predicted was coming to pass.  Let no man deceive you by any means, for that day shall not come, except there come  a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of predition.  And you do not warn people about a night, unless a morning is meant to follow.  A falling away only makes sense if there is something to fall back to.  A truth that can be restored brought back and lit again.  So this hard little verse is really a quiet promise.  The dimming was foretold, which means the returning was always part of the plan.  So the only question is a hopeful one.  When the light is offered again, will you know it, and take hold?  Paul warned that a falling away would come first.  Not because God failed, but because he foretold it.  And what is foretold can be restored.  When the light returns, will you take hold of it?

build-156-famine-of-hearing.heard: The prophet Amos gave his people a strange warning.  A famine is coming, he said.  But not the kind you are picturing.  There would be bread on the tables and water in the wells, and still the land would starve.  It would be a famine of a different kind, a hunger for the word of God, a time when the  living voice from heaven grew scarce, and people ached for it without always knowing what  the ache even was.  You could go about your days, eat your fill, and still feel a hollow place inside that  no meal could reach, a quiet starving of the soul for something true and living from God.  Behold, the days come, set the Lord God that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine  of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord.  And when people feel that kind of hunger, they do what hungry people do.  They go looking.  They search high and low, near and far, hoping to stumble on the thing that will finally  fill them.  Amos saw them wandering from one end of the world to the other, running here and there,  facing every rumor of where the word of God might still be found.  But in a famine of the word, the seeking alone does not satisfy.  They looked and looked and could not lay hold of it, because what they were hungry for had  grown rare in the land.  And they shall wander from sea to sea, and from the North even to the East, they shall run  to and fro to seek the word of the Lord, and shall not find it.  But think about what that hunger really means.  You do not egg for what was never real.  The very fact that a soul can starve for God's word is proof that such a word exists, and  that it was always meant to be found.  So a famine is never the end of the story.  It is the egg that comes right before the harvest.  God does not leave his people hungry forever, so the only question is a hopeful one.  When the word is set before you again, will you sit down and eat?  Amos foretold a famine, not of bread, but of hearing the word of God.  Yet a hunger like that is a promise.  You only starve for what is real.  When the word is offered again, will you feed on it?

build-157-marvellous-work.heard: The prophet Isaiah painted a strange, almost sad picture of his people.  The truth of God, he said, had become to them like a book that is sealed shut right there  in their hands, and yet closed its meaning locked away.  Imagine a precious book clasped and sealed that no one around can open.  Everyone senses it matters.  No one can get inside it.  The words of heaven sitting sealed in the middle of them.  So they carry it to their most educated man.  The scholar everyone respects, and they say, please read this for us.  He turns it over in his hands and has to admit the plain truth.  He cannot.  It is sealed.  And the vision of all has become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed, which  men deliver to one that is learned, saying, read this, I pray thee, and he saith I cannot,  for it is sealed.  Then they hand it to a plain, unschooled man, hoping simple honesty might succeed where  learning failed.  But he only shakes his head kindly.  Neither the wise nor the simple can open it on their own.  Wherefore the Lord said?  For as much as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honor me,  but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept  of men.  Isaiah saw the deeper trouble underneath.  The people still said the right words and kept the outward forms, honoring God with their  lips.  But their hearts had quietly drifted far away, and their worship had shrunk to habits taught  by men.  And no amount of human cleverness was going to fix that.  The wisdom of the wise had run to the very end of itself.  The experts had no key for a sealed book, or for a heart that had wandered off.  Therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvelous work among these people, even a marvelous  work and a wonder, for the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the understanding  of their prudent men shall be hid.  So God promised to step in himself and do something marvelous, a genuine wonder.  Not one more lecture from the learned, but an act of God that would open what men had  sealed and reach hearts that had wandered.  That is the beautiful turn in this verse.  When human wisdom hits its limit, God is only getting started.  He is fond of marvelous works and wonders.  The very things the experts said could not happen.  So the only question is a hopeful one.  When the wonder comes, will you be humble enough to receive it?  When human wisdom runs dry and the book is sealed, God promises a marvelous work and  a wonder, opening what men could not, and reaching hearts that had wandered.  When the wonder comes, will you receive it?

build-158-two-sticks.heard: Among the exiles by the river, the prophet Ezekiel received an unusual assignment from  God, not a sermon to preach, but an object lesson to act out, so plain that anyone watching  could understand it.  Take a stick, God told him, a flat wooden writing rod, and mark it with a name, for Judah,  and for the people gathered with him.  On record, belonging to one part of God's scattered family.  Then take a second stick, God said, and mark it with another name, for Joseph.  A separate record, belonging to another branch of the same family, long divided from the first.  Moreover, thou son of man, take thee one stick, and write upon it, for Judah, and for the children  of Israel his companions.  Then take another stick, and write upon it, for Joseph, the stick of E. E. Freyheim, and  for all the house of Israel his companions.  And join them one to another into one stick, and they shall become one in thine hand.  Now here is the part that made people stop and stare.  Using the two sticks together, God said, and join them, until the two become a single  stick, one solid piece, held together in your hand.  Two separate records, from two separated peoples, brought together and made one, not  one erasing the other, but the two joined, each completing the other, speaking now with  a single united voice.  And of course the people came asking, what do you mean by this?  Why two sticks made one?  What are you trying to show us?  God had built the question right into the lesson.  Say unto them, Thus set the Lord God, Behold, I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in  the hand of E.E. Freyheim, and the tribes of Israel his fellows, and will put them with  Him, even the stick of Judah, and make them one stick, and they shall be one in mine  hand.  Notice whose hand does the joining.  God says, They shall be one in mine hand.  He is the one who gathers the scattered records, and the scattered people, and binds them together  into one.  So this strange little sign is really a promise of gathering.  God does not leave His family, or His words to them, broken into separate pieces forever.  He brings them back together.  So the only question is a hopeful one.  When the two are made one in His hand, will you take them both up and read?  God had Ezekiel joined two records into one stick, two witnesses made one in His hand.  He gathers what was scattered, and binds His words together.  When the two are one, will you take them both up and read?

build-159-other-sheep.heard: On a hillside, surrounded by his listeners, Jesus reached for the most familiar picture  they had, a shepherd and his flock.  He was the shepherd, he told them, the good one, and the sheep were his very own.  It is a tender thing to be known like that, not counted as part of a crowd, but known,  which one, by name, by voice, by the particular way it strays and the particular way it finds  its way home.  And the knowing runs both ways.  His own know him too, the sound of his voice, the shape of his care, the way sheep will lift  their heads at one familiar step and follow no stranger.  I am the good shepherd and know my sheep and am known of mine.  But then Jesus said something that must have stopped them cold.  This flock, right here in front of me, he told them, you are not all the sheep I have.  There are others in other places not of this fold.  People they had never met, in lands they had never seen, who also belonged to him and were  waiting to be brought in.  And about them he made a quiet, sweeping promise, they too shall hear my voice.  Not two rival flocks, not one favored and one forgotten.  In the end one fold and one shepherd, every scattered sheep gathered home under the same  gentle hand. build-160-stone-cut.heard: The king of Babylon had a dream that troubled him deeply, and none of his wise men could  tell him what it meant, so a young exile named Daniel, who served the God of Heaven,  was brought in to explain it. So the only question is a hopeful one.  When that kingdom is offered to you, will you belong to it? build-161-called-of-god.heard: In ancient Israel, one man stood between the people and God. But an office that holy could not simply be claimed.  However, sincere a man was, however gifted, he could not reach out and take it for himself.  You cannot hand this to yourself.  It has to be given.  And no man takeeth this honor unto himself, but he that is called of God as was Aaron.  Think of how Aaron became High Priest.  He did not campaign for it or seize it.  God named him, and Moses brought him before the people and set him apart.  The honor came down to him.  It was never something he grasped.  And notice how it was done.  Not with the ceremony he arranged for himself.  But with another man's hands laid on his head, ordaining him.  The authority passed by touch and blessing, from someone who already held it.  Then the holy oil was poured over him, running down, and Aaron was consecrated, set apart,  given.  Everything about that day says the same thing.  This was received, not taken. build-162-keys-of-kingdom.heard: Far to the north, at a rocky place called Caesarea Philippi, Jesus stopped with his  disciples and put a piercing question to them.  Who do you say that I am? His Father in heaven had.  Then Jesus said something that would change Simon's life.  He gave him a new name.  Peter, which means a rock, and told him that on rock like that, solid and sure, he would  build something mint to outlast the ages. build-163-apostles-prophets.heard: The people Paul was riding to had once been outsiders, foreigners, strangers, on the far  edge of God's promises, with no place at the table and no share in the family. Men God had called and taught, whose witness became the solid ground the whole structure  would stand on.  And at the most important place of all, the cornerstone, the stone that sets the angle,  holds two walls together, and keeps the whole building square and true, stood Christ Himself. So the church was never meant to be a loose, shapeless crowd. So the only question is a hopeful one.  When He offers you a place in it, will you come inside? build-164-unity-of-faith.heard: When the risen Lord returned to heaven, He did not leave His church leaderless and on its own. Here is the quiet study, Jim. If those leaders were given until we all arrive at that unity, and the church has plainly not arrived yet, then the gifts were never meant to be temporary. build-165-laying-on-hands.heard: A wave of faith had swept through Samaria.  Whole crowds had heard the good news, believed it with glad hearts, and been baptized in water. They sent two of their own number, Peter and John, to go down in person. build-167-chosen-ordained.heard: The people God calls to his work rarely go looking for the honor. build-168-born-water-spirit.heard: Nicodemus was a ruler and a respected teacher, a man near the top of his world. Surely no one could climb back and start his life over from the beginning.  But the new birth was never meant to be physical. build-169-fulfil-righteousness.heard: Something startling happens at the very start of it all.  Jesus, who had no sin to wash away, walks down to the river Jordan and asks John to baptize  him. build-170-sacrament-worthily.heard: Paul was handing on something sacred that he had received himself.  On the very night he was betrayed, at supper with his friends. This one, he said, was the sign of a new covenant,  a solemn promise sealed between God and his people and offered freely to them. Here is the quiet study, Jim.  This is why it is done again and again and never just once. build-172-gospel-preached-to-the-dead.heard: Some who heard the good news had already died before they could finish their lives in the body. build-177-make-me-a-sanctuary.heard: While Israel camped in the wilderness, the Lord gave Moses a strange instruction,  Have the people build me a sanctuary? build-178-in-our-image.heard: At the start of all things, before any person drew breath, a council happened in the Godhead.  Let us make man in our image. build-18-emmaus.heard: It was the same Sunday. The tomb was empty, the rumors were flying, and two of Jesus'  followers had given up and left.
